interactions.label: Why are antipyretics such as paracetamol effective in fever but not in hyperther

params.question: Why are antipyretics such as paracetamol effective in fever but not in hyperthermia?

answers.text: Paracetamol directly stimulates sweating, which only occurs when the hypothalamic thermostat is intact

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Paracetamol works by blocking cyclo-oxygenase-2 in the hypothalamus, not by stimulating sweating. Its mechanism targets the prostaglandin E2 pathway that raises the set-point in fever.

answers.text: In fever, prostaglandin E2 raises the hypothalamic set-point via COX-2, and antipyretics block this pathway; in hyperthermia, PGE2 is not driving the temperature rise

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In fever the pathway is: exogenous pyrogen → macrophage cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α) → COX-2 → PGE2 → set-point elevation. Antipyretics interrupt this at COX-2. In hyperthermia PGE2 plays no role, so blocking COX-2 has no therapeutic target.

answers.text: Antipyretics are metabolised too rapidly at temperatures above 40°C to exert any effect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Antipyretic metabolism is not meaningfully altered by high body temperature. The reason they fail in hyperthermia is that PGE2-mediated set-point elevation is not the mechanism of the temperature rise.

answers.text: Hyperthermia permanently damages the hypothalamus, preventing any pharmacological intervention

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While severe hyperthermia can cause neuronal injury, the reason antipyretics fail is simpler: the temperature rise is not driven by PGE2, so blocking COX-2 has no therapeutic target. Physical cooling is needed instead.

overallFeedback.feedback: In fever, exogenous pyrogens trigger macrophage cytokines (IL-1β, IL-6, TNF-α), which activate COX-2 in the hypothalamus to produce PGE2, raising the set-point. Antipyretics block COX-2, reducing PGE2 and lowering the set-point. In hyperthermia PGE2 is not involved, so antipyretics have no target — only physical cooling works.

Exactly right. In fever, prostaglandin E2 is the key mediator that raises the hypothalamic set-point. Antipyretics block COX-2 to reduce PGE2, lowering the set-point back to normal. In hyperthermia the set-point was never raised, so this entire pathway is irrelevant — physical cooling is the treatment.

params.question: Why can a temperature of 37.9°C with confusion in an elderly diabetic patient indicate greater clinical danger than 40.5°C in a young athlete?

answers.text: The elderly have a lower baseline body temperature, so any rise above 37°C is always abnormal

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While baseline temperature may be slightly lower in the elderly, that is not the key reason. The critical factor is their blunted immune response, which masks the severity of the underlying infection.

answers.text: Young athletes can safely tolerate temperatures up to 42°C without organ damage

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. No individual can safely tolerate 42°C. The teaching point is that a blunted febrile response in the elderly masks the severity of the underlying infection — a modest rise may represent septic shock.

answers.text: A blunted immune response in the elderly means even a modest temperature elevation can signal severe infection such as septic shock

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The elderly mount an attenuated febrile response due to reduced cytokine production. A temperature of 37.9°C with altered sensorium may represent septic shock, while a young immunocompetent patient with a higher fever may have a less critical underlying cause.

answers.text: Confusion in elderly patients is always caused by medication side effects rather than infection

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Confusion in the elderly has many causes including infection. The key teaching point is that the host's immune status modifies how fever presents — a blunted response can mask life-threatening infection.

overallFeedback.feedback: In elderly or immunocompromised patients, the immune system produces fewer endogenous pyrogens, resulting in a blunted febrile response. A temperature of 37.9°C with confusion can therefore signal septic shock. Always assess the host alongside the temperature — treat the patient, not the number.

Correct. The clinical pearl is: treat the patient, not the temperature number. A blunted immune response means fever may be minimal even in severe sepsis, making clinical signs like confusion more diagnostically important than the thermometer reading.

interactions.label: A 35-year-old farmer from rural Meghalaya presents with high-grade fever for fiv

params.question: A 35-year-old farmer from rural Meghalaya presents with high-grade fever for five days. During a thorough skin examination, you find a painless, dark, crusted lesion in the left axillary fold. This finding is most characteristic of:

answers.text: Scrub typhus eschar

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The painless, dark, crusted eschar in a concealed body fold is pathognomonic of scrub typhus. Present in 50–70% of Indian cases, it hides in the axillae, groins, scalp, behind the ears, and between the toes — only a complete skin inspection will find it.

answers.text: Cutaneous anthrax

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Anthrax eschars typically appear on exposed skin (hands, face, neck) at the site of inoculation. The axillary location and concealed nature of this lesion, combined with the rural febrile presentation, point to scrub typhus.

answers.text: Primary chancre of syphilis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A syphilitic chancre is painless but typically appears at the site of sexual inoculation (genitalia, oral mucosa). The rural occupational exposure and febrile illness with a lesion in the axillary fold are classic for scrub typhus.

answers.text: Tubercular cold abscess

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Tubercular cold abscesses are fluctuant, non-tender swellings, not crusted eschars. They present differently from the discrete, dark, crusted lesion described here.

overallFeedback.feedback: The painless, dark, crusted eschar in a body fold (axilla, groin, scalp, behind ears, between toes) is pathognomonic of scrub typhus. Present in 50–70% of Indian cases, it is the single most valuable bedside finding — but only a complete skin inspection will find it.

Well done. The scrub typhus eschar clinches the diagnosis at the bedside — start doxycycline on clinical grounds. It is painless and hides in body folds, which is why undressing the patient fully for a complete skin inspection is mandatory in every febrile evaluation.

interactions.label: Two patients each have a weakly positive Widal test at the same titre. Patient A

params.question: Two patients each have a weakly positive Widal test at the same titre. Patient A is an urban software engineer with no travel history and two days of low-grade fever. Patient B has step-ladder fever and recently returned from a rural endemic area. How should these identical results be interpreted?

answers.text: Both results are diagnostic of enteric fever and warrant antibiotic treatment

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. A weakly positive Widal has different significance depending on the clinical context. Without a compatible clinical picture and epidemiological risk, a weak positive is likely non-specific reactivity.

answers.text: Neither result is clinically useful; blood cultures should be the sole basis for diagnosis

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While blood cultures are the gold standard, serological tests like Widal are interpreted alongside clinical probability. Patient B's result, combined with the clinical picture, adds real diagnostic weight.

answers.text: The result in Patient A is likely a false positive, while in Patient B it is clinically significant due to higher pre-test probability

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. This is Bayes' theorem at the bedside. The same test result carries different predictive value depending on the pre-test probability. Patient B's step-ladder fever and endemic exposure create a high pre-test probability, making the weakly positive Widal clinically meaningful.

answers.text: The result in Patient B is less reliable because endemic exposure increases the chance of non-specific cross-reactivity

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While cross-reactivity exists, endemic exposure combined with a compatible clinical picture (step-ladder fever) increases the pre-test probability for enteric fever, making a positive Widal more significant, not less.

overallFeedback.feedback: Pre-test probability determines the meaning of any test result. A weakly positive Widal in a low-risk patient (no compatible symptoms, no endemic exposure) is likely non-specific. The same result in a patient with step-ladder fever from an endemic area is clinically significant. Always interpret investigations against the clinical picture.

Exactly right. Pre-test probability, shaped by clinical features and epidemiological context, determines how any test result should be interpreted. The same titre is noise in one patient and a confirmatory finding in another — that is Bayes' theorem in clinical practice.

interactions.label: Compared to Western series, Indian fever of unknown origin has a distinct aetiol

params.question: Compared to Western series, Indian fever of unknown origin has a distinct aetiological profile. Which statement best describes this difference?

answers.text: Malignancies are more common in Indian FUO than in Western series, accounting for over 35% of cases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Malignancies account for only 15–20% of Indian FUO, with lymphoma as the most common malignant cause. The dominant category in Indian FUO is infections.

answers.text: Inflammatory causes account for the majority in both Indian and Western series

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Inflammatory causes (mainly adult-onset Still disease and SLE) account for 20–25% of Indian FUO — a significant proportion but not the majority. Infections are the leading category.

answers.text: Drug fever is the leading cause of Indian FUO, accounting for over 30% of cases

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Drug fever falls in the miscellaneous category, which accounts for a small proportion of FUO. In Indian series, infections dominate the aetiological profile.

answers.text: Infections dominate Indian FUO at 35–40%, led by extrapulmonary tuberculosis, whereas infections are far less prominent in Western series

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. In Indian FUO series, infections account for 35–40% of cases, with extrapulmonary tuberculosis as the leading cause, followed by endocarditis, kala-azar, and brucellosis. This infection-dominant profile differs markedly from Western data and directly shapes the initial diagnostic approach.

overallFeedback.feedback: In Indian FUO series, infections lead at 35–40%, with extrapulmonary tuberculosis as the commonest cause. Inflammatory conditions (mainly adult-onset Still disease and SLE) follow at 20–25%, and malignancies (mainly lymphoma) at 15–20%. This infection-dominant profile differs from Western series and should guide the initial workup.

Correct. The Indian FUO profile is infection-dominant, with extrapulmonary TB as the leading cause. This has direct implications — always prioritise TB, kala-azar, and endocarditis in the initial workup of an Indian patient with FUO.

interactions.label: During a fever of unknown origin workup, a colleague suggests starting empiric c

params.question: During a fever of unknown origin workup, a colleague suggests starting empiric corticosteroids because the patient's presentation suggests an inflammatory condition. What is the most important reason to withhold corticosteroids at this stage?

answers.text: Corticosteroids are ineffective against inflammatory causes of prolonged fever

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Corticosteroids ARE effective in many inflammatory conditions (SLE, adult-onset Still disease), which is precisely why the initial improvement is deceptive. The danger lies in what they do to undiagnosed infections lurking beneath the inflammatory picture.

answers.text: Tuberculosis and visceral leishmaniasis must be excluded first, as both worsen catastrophically under immunosuppression

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Empiric corticosteroids in a patient with undiagnosed TB or kala-azar cause disease flare and can be fatal. The initial clinical improvement is deceptive — it reflects suppression of the immune response, not disease control. Always exclude these infections before starting immunosuppressive therapy.

answers.text: Corticosteroids interfere with blood culture sensitivity and make microbiological diagnosis impossible

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. While immunosuppression can affect some test results, the critical danger is clinical: undiagnosed tuberculosis and kala-azar worsen catastrophically under corticosteroids. The initial improvement is deceptive.

answers.text: Empiric treatment of any kind is always contraindicated in fever of unknown origin

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Empiric treatment IS appropriate in specific FUO settings — for example, neutropenic FUO requires immediate broad-spectrum antibiotics, and febrile neutropenia demands antibiotics within one hour. The specific concern here is about corticosteroids masking and worsening TB or kala-azar.

overallFeedback.feedback: In Indian FUO, tuberculosis and visceral leishmaniasis are common causes. Both worsen catastrophically under corticosteroids — the initial clinical improvement is deceptive and reflects immune suppression, not disease control. Always exclude TB and kala-azar before starting empiric corticosteroids.

Correct. TB and kala-azar are leading causes of FUO in India, and both worsen dramatically under immunosuppression. The initial improvement with steroids is deceptive — never start empiric corticosteroids without first excluding these infections.
